title: Three Churches: Asleep, Faithful, Lukewarm
overview: Jesus sends messages to three churches in what is now western Turkey: Sardis, alive in name only; Philadelphia, weak but faithful; and Laodicea, rich but complacent.

parts.label: Sardis: alive in name only (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: This church has a good reputation but is close to dead, and it is told to wake up or Jesus will arrive without warning, the way a thief comes. The few who have kept their clothes clean, likely a picture of staying faithful, are promised white clothes and a name kept in the book of life, pictured like a city's list of its citizens.

parts.label: Philadelphia: weak but loyal (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: Jesus holds the key of David, recalling Isaiah 22, where a royal steward is given the palace key and decides who may enter. This small church has little strength but has stayed loyal, and the door set open before it is read either as a way into God's kingdom or as a chance to spread its message.

parts.label: A bitter local conflict (v. 9)
parts.note: Many scholars see a painful split here between a small group of Jesus followers, likely including Jewish members, and the city's synagogue, with each side claiming to be God's true people. Lines like this were later twisted to fuel hatred of Jewish people, a use most churches today firmly reject.

parts.label: The hour of trial (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Some Christians, especially in certain Protestant groups, read the promise to be kept from the coming hour of trial as being taken away before a final time of worldwide suffering, while many others read it as being kept safe through it. In a city often shaken by earthquakes, the faithful are promised to stand as a permanent pillar in God's temple, marked with God's name and the name of the new Jerusalem.

parts.label: Laodicea: lukewarm and self-satisfied (vv. 14-18)
parts.note: Many scholars link the lukewarm image to the city's tepid piped water, unlike the useful hot and cold springs nearby, while older readers took cold to mean open rejection. This wealthy city, known for banking and wool, thinks it needs nothing, but Jesus calls it poor, blind and naked and offers real gold, white clothes and ointment for its eyes.

parts.label: Knocking at the door (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: The hard words are framed as love, and Jesus pictures himself knocking, ready to come in and share a meal with anyone who opens. The line is often used as an invitation to individuals, but it is first spoken to a church that has left him outside, and whoever stands firm is promised a seat with him on his throne.

disagreement: Most Christians read these letters as messages to real first century churches that also speak to every church, while some, especially in certain Protestant traditions, also see the seven churches as stages of church history, with Laodicea standing for the final age before Jesus returns.
think: Where might your reputation, or your own picture of yourself, differ from what is actually going on underneath?
